accepted.question_text: Can one develop a systematic, preferably computer-algebraic, method for evaluating the multi-loop thermal sum-integrals that arise in perturbative finite-temperature QCD and related finite-temperature field theories, instead of continuing to solve the needed master sum-integrals one case at a time? Such a method would need to work in the presence of discretized Matsubara frequencies and the additional temperature scale, reuse more of the analytic machinery that is successful at zero temperature than integration-by-parts relations alone, and provide a reusable way to separate ultraviolet and infrared divergent pieces so that higher-order perturbative computations can be streamlined.
accepted.context_brief: Systematic treatment of multi-loop thermal sum-integrals

evidence.quote: the problem of evaluating the resulting set of master sum-integrals still presents a formidable challenge.
the few sum-integrals that have been computed beyond the 2-loop level have been solved on a case-by-case basis

let us express our hope that a further generalization of the techniques presented here and possibly an automatization of the subtraction procedure will lead towards a computer-algebraic treatment of multi-loop sum-integrals, in order to greatly streamline higher-order perturbative computations in finite-temperature field theories.

accepted.question_text: Can the four convergent three-loop sum-integral contributions B^I_N, B^II_N, B^III_N, and B^IV_N that remain after the subtraction procedure be evaluated analytically for general integer N, rather than only by numerical approximation at specific fixed values such as N = 2 and N = 3? In concrete terms, the open problem is to turn the one-dimensional integral representations obtained after the subtraction and coordinate-space transformations into general-N formulas or a comparably systematic evaluation procedure that avoids case-by-case numerical treatment.
accepted.context_brief: General-N evaluation of the residual sum-integrals

evidence.quote: While it would be most desirable to obtain expressions for B I−IV N for general N, in practice we are forced to evaluate them at fixed N.
This leaves us with one-dimensional integrals over products of polylogarithms, logarithms and hyperbolic functions.
